title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals are using generative AI to impersonate real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney, to conduct voice and identity fraud against victims in Georgia and South Florida. The scams combine deepfakes, voice cloning, phone spoofing, and fake photographs to make fraudulent requests appear authentic. These deployed systems are not systems built by their supposed operators, but tools repurposed entirely outside their intended use by bad actors to deceive.

The failure to catch these scams in real time sits with the communication platforms and financial institutions through which the fraud flows. A person who receives a call from what appears to be a known attorney or family member currently has no reliable way to verify authenticity before sending money, and reversing a transfer after the fact is difficult. What would have caught many of these scams: stronger verification procedures for urgent money requests, caller identity verification that cannot be spoofed, and freezes on rapid fund transfers.

It is not established whether the generative AI systems themselves were modified or whether they were used as provided by their creators.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create deepfakes and clone voices to steal money from victims across Georgia and South Florida. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to target immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints totaling more than $10.4 million.

Criminals are using generative AI to make traditional scams more convincing by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photographs, and researching victims' family relationships. Common scams include the grandparent scam, romance schemes, and fake investment opportunities. To protect themselves, people should establish code words to verify loved ones' identities, verify urgent requests by calling directly, never send money based solely on phone calls, and report suspected scams to law enforcement. Experts warn that as AI tools become cheaper and more accessible, verification rather than quick action will be consumers' best defense.
